summary: Defines EAP-GPSK, a lightweight Extensible Authentication Protocol method based on a shared key that supports mutual authentication and key derivation. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Two sides who already know the same secret word prove it to each other, and then use it to make fresh secret keys, without needing heavy tools.

questions: does eap-gpsk protect against dictionary attacks
subtitle: A lightweight way for two parties that already share a secret key to prove it to each other and derive fresh session keys.

tldr.problem: Devices with limited processing power, memory and battery need an EAP authentication method that avoids public key cryptography but still authenticates both sides and produces keys.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-GPSK exchanges random nonces and identities in four messages (GPSK-1 to GPSK-4). Each side proves knowledge of the pre-shared key with a MAC over the exchanged values, and both derive session keys from the same inputs.
tldr.outcome: It gives mutual authentication, integrity protection, replay protection and exported MSK and EMSK keys using only symmetric cryptography, but it offers no protection against dictionary attacks on weak keys and no perfect forward secrecy.

facts.label: Messages
facts.value: GPSK-1 to GPSK-4, plus two failure messages

today: RFC 5433 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3748 and the EAP key management framework in RFC 5247.

sections.title: Goals of EAP-GPSK
sections.content:
RFC 5433 defines EAP-GPSK, an EAP method built on a generalized pre-shared key. Mutual authentication comes from a nonce-based exchange that is secured by the pre-shared key.

The listed design goals are simplicity, a security model where the attacker has full control over the communication channel, efficiency, flexibility and extensibility. It uses no public key cryptography and relies fully on symmetric cryptography, which keeps the computational cost low for devices with limited processing power, memory and battery. The server proposes a list of ciphersuites and the client picks one. Protected data fields can carry extra information such as channel binding data.
sections.eli5: Two friends share a secret handshake. This method lets them check each other's handshake using only simple tools, so even a tiny gadget can do it.

sections.title: The Four-Message Exchange
sections.content:
After the usual EAP identity exchange, the server starts the method and the two sides swap four messages. In GPSK-1 the server sends its identity ID_Server, a random number RAND_Server and a list of supported ciphersuites. In GPSK-2 the peer sends its own identity and random number, repeats what it received, names the ciphersuite it selected and adds a Message Authentication Code (MAC) over all of it.

The server checks that MAC and the consistency of the identities, nonces and ciphersuite parameters. If they check out, it answers with GPSK-3, carrying its own MAC over the session parameters. The peer verifies that MAC and replies with GPSK-4, which the server follows with an EAP Success. Each MAC is keyed with a key derived from the pre-shared key, so a valid MAC counts as proof of possession of that key.

GPSK-2 and GPSK-3 can also carry encrypted protected data, and GPSK-4 can carry the peer's protected data. Two further messages, GPSK-Fail and GPSK-Protected-Fail, handle errors. Which ciphersuites to offer and pick is a matter of policy and implementation, outside the RFC's scope.
sections.eli5: The server and the device each toss a secret random number into the pot, then each one shows a stamp that only someone holding the shared secret could make. When both stamps match, they trust each other.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Key Management
sections.content:
The long-term PSK SHOULD be a strong key of at least 16 octets. A password or passphrase is NOT RECOMMENDED because EAP-GPSK is vulnerable to dictionary attacks. The management interface MUST let administrators enter PSKs up to 64 octets as ASCII strings and in hexadecimal, and ID_Peer and ID_Server MUST be provisioned with the PSK.

From the PSK, the nonces, the identities and the selected ciphersuite, both sides derive a Master Key MK. From MK they derive the exported MSK and EMSK (each 64 octets), plus a session key SK that proves knowledge of the PSK and, with an encrypting ciphersuite, a key PK that protects the protected data. The RFC also defines the Method-ID, Session-ID, Peer-ID and Server-ID values that the EAP key management framework requires.
sections.eli5: The shared secret is like a master recipe. Each time they meet, they mix in fresh random ingredients and cook up brand new keys, so yesterday's keys are never reused.

sections.title: Ciphersuites and the GKDF
sections.content:
A ciphersuite combines an encryption algorithm, a key derivation function and a MAC. Two are defined. Ciphersuite 1 (0x0001) uses AES-CBC-128 for encryption and AES-CMAC-128 for integrity, with a key size of 16 and a MAC length of 16 octets. It MUST be implemented. Ciphersuite 2 (0x0002) uses NULL encryption and HMAC-SHA256, with a key size and MAC length of 32 octets. It MAY be implemented.

Both use the Generalized Key Derivation Function (GKDF), which builds output by concatenating MAC outputs over a counter and the input string, then truncating to the length needed. Ciphersuite 2 does no encryption, so it MUST NOT be used if confidential information appears in the protected data. The RFC recommends provisioning 256-bit keys in all cases.
sections.eli5: A ciphersuite is a toolbox. One toolbox can lock messages and stamp them. The other can only stamp them, so you must not put secrets in it.

sections.title: Packet Formats
sections.content:
Every EAP-GPSK packet has the standard EAP Code, Identifier, Length and Type fields, followed by an 8-bit OP-Code that says which message follows, then the payload. The OP-Codes are 0x01 to 0x06 for GPSK-1, GPSK-2, GPSK-3, GPSK-4, GPSK-Fail and GPSK-Protected-Fail, with 0x00 reserved.

Ciphersuites are 6-octet values: a 4-octet vendor field (0x00000000 for IETF-defined suites) and a 2-octet specifier. Protected data travels as type-length-value triples. With an encrypting ciphersuite the block also holds an initialization vector and padding; without encryption the IV length and pad length fields are still present and set to 0.
sections.eli5: Every message wears a little name tag that says which step of the conversation it belongs to, so the other side knows how to read it.

sections.title: Failures and Packet Processing
sections.content:
Any packet that cannot be parsed, or that arrives unexpectedly, MUST be silently discarded. A packet whose MAC fails is also silently discarded by the peer (for GPSK-3) or the server (for GPSK-4). GPSK-1 has no MAC protection, so a properly parsed GPSK-1 MUST be accepted; if the peer has no ciphersuite in common, or does not want to authenticate to that server, it MUST answer with an EAP-NAK.

For GPSK-2, an unknown user gets a GPSK-Fail with "PSK Not Found" or "Authentication Failure", depending on policy, and a failed MAC gets "Authentication Failure". If the MAC is correct but the peer is not authorized, the server sends a GPSK-Protected-Fail with "Authorization Failure". The failure codes are 0x00000001 to 0x00000003.
sections.eli5: If a message looks wrong or its stamp does not match, the receiver just ignores it, like tossing out a letter with a fake signature.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC claims shared-key authentication, ciphersuite negotiation, mutual authentication, integrity protection, replay protection, key derivation and session independence. Because both nonces are random and RAND_Server is 32 octets long, the RFC says one expects to have to record 2**64 successful authentications before a run could be replayed.

It also lists what it does not provide: no dictionary attack protection, no fast reconnect, no fragmentation, no identity protection, and no perfect forward secrecy, so a compromised PSK exposes recorded past sessions and allows impersonation. It cannot claim confidentiality per RFC 3748 because it lacks identity protection. Protected failure messages help debugging but let an attacker learn whether an ID_Peer is a valid user, so they can be disabled. The PSK must be shared only between one peer and one server.
sections.eli5: It is strong when the secret is long and random, but a short guessable secret is like a weak padlock, and if the secret leaks, old recordings can be opened too.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA allocated EAP Type 51 for EAP-GPSK and created registries for ciphersuites, protected data payload types, failure codes and op-codes. New values can be added or modified through IETF Review. Each new ciphersuite must give processing rules and say how encryption, integrity, key derivation and key length are instantiated.
sections.eli5: There is an official list where new kinds of tools and message types get written down, so everyone uses the same numbers.
